::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives" icon="false"}
After this lecture (and Lab 4) you can:

1. **represent** facts as (head, relation, tail) triples, explain RDF, ontologies, and the open- vs closed-world assumptions — and say which one your data license actually grants you;
2. **define** the TransE, DistMult, ComplEx, and RotatE scoring functions and compute each by hand on toy embeddings;
3. **prove** which relation patterns — symmetry, antisymmetry, inversion, composition, 1-to-N — each model can represent: the model-selection cheat sheet;
4. **derive** the margin-based and self-adversarial negative-sampling losses and explain corruption sampling under the open-world assumption;
5. **run** filtered ranking evaluation, compute MRR and Hits@K by hand, and explain why FB15k had to become FB15k-237.
:::

## The graph that completes itself

In 2012 Google announced it would stop searching for *strings* and start searching for
*things*: behind the search box it had built a graph of entities — people, places,
proteins, films — connected by named relations. Wikidata, the open sibling, now holds
over a hundred million entities and more than a billion statements, each one a triple
you already met in Lab 1: *(Innopolis University, located_in, Innopolis)*.

Here is the industry's dirty secret, and this week's engine. When researchers audited
Freebase — the KG that seeded Google's — they found that **71% of its people had no
recorded place of birth**, and 75% no nationality. Not because these facts are unknown
to humanity; because nobody had typed them in. Every real knowledge graph is a sparse
shadow of the truth it models.

::: {.predict}
**Commit before you look.** Our own twelve-triple fragment from Lab 1 — is it complete?
Find a true fact about its ten entities that none of the twelve triples states, using
only facts already derivable from the fragment itself.

::: {.predict-answer}
**(IU, located_in, Tatarstan)** — because IU is in Innopolis and Innopolis is in
Tatarstan. (Also: KFU is in Tatarstan; both universities are in Russia; Kazan is in
Russia…) The fragment *implies* far more than it *states*. A knowledge graph that could
score unstated triples by plausibility would complete itself — and that scoring
problem, **knowledge graph completion**, is this week.
:::
:::

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-hero.html >}}

Last week's cliffhanger asked what happens when edges get types and directions. The
honest answer: everything from Week 3 survives — encoder, decoder, similarity, loss —
but the decoder must grow up. "Are these two entities close?" is no longer the
question; *(Kazan, capital_of, Tatarstan)* is true while *(Kazan, part_of, Volga)* is
nonsense, and both pairs are "close". The question is now **"is this fact true?"**, and
the decoder must hear the relation to answer it.

**Roadmap.** (1) Facts, schemas, and the open-world assumption — the epistemics of
knowledge. (2) Completion as a ranking task. (3) Four geometries for truth: relations
as translations, products, complex products, rotations. (4) The cheat sheet: what each
geometry can and cannot say, with proofs. (5) Training when missing ≠ false. (6)
Evaluation that doesn't lie: filtered MRR, and two famous scandals.

::: {.callout-note title="Recap — what this lecture assumes" collapse="true"}
- **Lab 1**: the twelve Wikidata triples and `kg_stats` — entities are everything that appears as a head *or* a tail, including "city" and "university".
- **Week 3**: the encoder–decoder template; embedding lookup tables; negative sampling (SGNS); Pitfall 2 (only geometry is identifiable, not coordinates).
- **Week 1**: heterogeneous graphs — typed nodes and edges as a modeling decision. A KG is that decision taken seriously at planetary scale.
:::

## 1. Facts, schemas, and honest ignorance

A **knowledge graph** stores atomic facts as triples $(h, r, t)$: a head entity, a
named relation, a tail entity. The web-standard serialization is
<span class="term" data-def="RDF (Resource Description Framework): the W3C standard for publishing triples, with globally unique URIs for entities and relations so that independent datasets can merge without name collisions. Wikidata speaks it; so does every biomedical ontology.">**RDF**</span> —
subject–predicate–object with global URIs, so that *Kazan-the-city* never collides with
*Kazan-the-helicopter-plant* when two datasets merge. Above the facts sits an
<span class="term" data-def="Ontology / schema: the type system of a KG — entity classes (city, person), relation signatures (located_in: place → place), and constraints (a capital_of head must be a city). It is what makes some corruptions detectably absurd.">**ontology**</span>:
classes, relation signatures (*located_in* goes place → place), constraints. Our
fragment carries a miniature one — the `instance_of` edges *are* its type system.

The epistemological fine print matters more than any formula today:

::: {.callout-important title="The open-world assumption, or: what a missing edge means" icon="false"}
Under the <span class="term" data-def="Closed-world assumption (CWA): anything not stated is false. Correct for a database that is complete by construction — an airline's flight table. Catastrophically wrong for knowledge graphs.">closed-world assumption</span>,
absence is denial: no *(IU, located_in, Tatarstan)* edge means IU is *not* in
Tatarstan. Databases live here. Knowledge graphs cannot: they are built by volunteers
and extractors sampling an unbounded world, so absence usually means *nobody said*.
That is the <span class="term" data-def="Open-world assumption (OWA): a missing fact is unknown, not false. The working epistemics of every real KG — and the reason KG training data contains no true negatives, only unstated triples.">**open-world assumption**</span>,
and it has a sharp consequence for machine learning: **a KG gives you positives and
silence — never labeled negatives.** Every "negative example" this week is manufactured
by corrupting a positive, and some manufactured negatives will be accidentally true.
Keep that discomfort; §5 pays it off.
:::

Scale check, so the toy examples stay calibrated: Wikidata ≈ $10^8$ entities; Google's
graph reported 500 billion facts on 5 billion entities back in 2020; biomedical KGs
(drugs–targets–diseases) power literal drug discovery. At that scale, completion is not
a party trick — every percent of Hits@10 is millions of recovered facts.

## 2. Completion is ranking

The task, precisely. Given the training triples $\mathcal{T}$, learn a **scoring
function** $f(h, r, t) \in \mathbb{R}$ — higher means more plausible — and answer
queries $(h, r, ?)$ and $(?, r, t)$ by scoring *every* entity in the slot and ranking.
Nobody asks for calibrated probabilities of truth (the open world forbids them); a
ranking that puts real facts above fabrications is both achievable and useful.

In the Week 3 template: the **encoder** is still a lookup table — one vector per entity,
and now *one vector per relation*. The **similarity** is membership in $\mathcal{T}$.
All the invention concentrates in the **decoder** $f$, which must take *three* inputs.
The filing cabinet gains its promised row — and this whole lecture is the story of one
cell:

| method | encoder | decoder $f(h,r,t)$ | similarity |
|---|---|---|---|
| DeepWalk (Wk 3) | lookup | $\mathbf{z}_h^\top \mathbf{z}_t$ — relation-deaf | walk co-occurrence |
| **KG embeddings (today)** | lookup ×2 | **four designs below** | observed triples |
| GCN (Wk 6) | neural network | task head | labels |

## 3. Four geometries for "is this true?"

Each model is one answer to a single design question: *what kind of geometric object is
a relation?* All four are computed below on concrete toy vectors — check at least one
by hand now, because the midterm will ask for exactly this:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-scorers.html >}}

**TransE (2013): a relation is a translation.**
$$
f(h, r, t) = -\bigl\|\mathbf{h} + \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{t}\bigr\|
$$
True facts should make $\mathbf{h} + \mathbf{r}$ land on $\mathbf{t}$; the score is
the (negated) miss distance. One vector per relation, beautifully cheap, and
chains of translations *add* — a property §4 turns into a theorem. It is Week 3's
dot-product decoder with one added vector, and it started the entire field.

**DistMult (2015): a relation is a feature-weighting.**
$$
f(h, r, t) = \sum_{i=1}^{d} h_i \, r_i \, t_i
$$
A bilinear score with a diagonal relation matrix: $r$ decides which coordinates of the
head–tail agreement matter. Fast, strong on benchmarks — and hiding a flaw you can spot
from the formula alone: $h$ and $t$ enter symmetrically. Look at the figure's middle
panel: swapping them cannot change the score. *Ever.*

**ComplEx (2016): a relation is a complex weighting.** Move every vector to
$\mathbb{C}^d$ and score with the real part of the Hermitian product:
$$
f(h, r, t) = \operatorname{Re}\Bigl(\textstyle\sum_i h_i \, r_i \, \bar{t}_i\Bigr).
$$
The conjugate on $\bar{t}$ breaks the swap symmetry: the figure's third panel scores
$+2$ forward and $-2$ backward. One implementation detail with a proof-sized payoff:
choosing $\operatorname{Im}(\mathbf{r}) = 0$ recovers DistMult exactly — symmetry
becomes a *choice per relation* instead of a prison.

**RotatE (2019): a relation is a rotation.** Keep $\mathbb{C}^d$ but constrain
$|r_i| = 1$ — each relation coordinate is a pure phase, rotating the corresponding
head coordinate:
$$
f(h, r, t) = -\bigl\|\mathbf{h} \circ \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{t}\bigr\|,
\qquad \mathbf{h} \circ \mathbf{r} = (h_1 r_1, \ldots, h_d r_d).
$$
Translation's chaining, plus phases that can express symmetry (a half-turn is its own
inverse) — the best of both prior worlds, and the reason it tops this family's
benchmarks.

Formulas memorize poorly and derive well. Watch the first one *earn* its geometry — and
fail exactly where the algebra says it must:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w4-transe.html >}}

## 4. What a geometry can and cannot say

Here is the discipline that turns four formulas into an engineering decision. A
**relation pattern** is a logical regularity your relations obey; a model *represents*
the pattern if some parameter choice makes the pattern hold exactly in the scores. Five
patterns cover most of practice:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-patterns.html >}}

The verdicts are theorems, not folklore. The four you should be able to produce cold:

::: {#prp-transe-sym .proposition name="TransE cannot represent a symmetric relation"}
If $f(a, r, b) = f(b, r, a) = 0$ (both directions score perfectly) for some $a \neq b$,
then $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}$ — and the relation collapses: every entity is related
precisely to itself.
:::

<details><summary>Proof (two lines)</summary>
Perfect scores mean $\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{b}$ and
$\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{a}$. Adding: $2\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}$. With
$\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}$, $f(h,r,t) = -\|\mathbf{h} - \mathbf{t}\|$ is maximal only
at $\mathbf{t} = \mathbf{h}$. $\square$
</details>

::: {#prp-distmult-sym .proposition name="DistMult is symmetric — always"}
For every choice of parameters, $f(h, r, t) = f(t, r, h)$. DistMult cannot prefer
*(Kazan, capital_of, Tatarstan)* over *(Tatarstan, capital_of, Kazan)* by any margin,
for any training, ever.
:::

<details><summary>Proof (one line)</summary>
$\sum_i h_i r_i t_i = \sum_i t_i r_i h_i$ by commutativity of multiplication. $\square$
</details>

::: {#prp-complex .proposition name="ComplEx chooses its symmetry per relation"}
With $\operatorname{Im}(\mathbf{r}) = \mathbf{0}$ the ComplEx score is symmetric in
$(h,t)$; with $\operatorname{Im}(\mathbf{r}) \neq \mathbf{0}$ it contains an
antisymmetric term — so both symmetric and antisymmetric relations are representable,
relation by relation.
:::

<details><summary>Proof sketch (split into parts)</summary>
Write $h_i \bar t_i = s_i + a_i i$ where $s_i = \operatorname{Re}(h_i \bar t_i)$ is
symmetric under the swap $h \leftrightarrow t$ and $a_i = \operatorname{Im}(h_i \bar t_i)$
flips sign under it. Then
$\operatorname{Re}(r_i \, h_i \bar t_i) = \operatorname{Re}(r_i) s_i - \operatorname{Im}(r_i) a_i$:
the real part of $\mathbf{r}$ weights the symmetric channel, the imaginary part the
antisymmetric one. Set $\operatorname{Im}(\mathbf{r}) = 0$ for symmetry; give it mass
for direction — the figure's $+2/-2$ panel is this identity with numbers. $\square$
</details>

::: {#prp-rotate .proposition name="RotatE composes"}
If $r_3 = r_1 \circ r_2$ (phases add), then whenever $(a, r_1, b)$ and $(b, r_2, c)$
hold exactly, $(a, r_3, c)$ holds exactly: rotation is the only decoder here whose
relations form a group under composition.
:::

<details><summary>Proof (one line, plus the contrast)</summary>
$(\mathbf{a} \circ \mathbf{r_1}) \circ \mathbf{r_2} = \mathbf{a} \circ (\mathbf{r_1} \circ \mathbf{r_2})$
by associativity of (coordinatewise) complex multiplication; unit moduli are closed
under it. TransE composes the same way with $\mathbf{r_3} = \mathbf{r_1} + \mathbf{r_2}$
— but cannot simultaneously do symmetry (@prp-transe-sym); DistMult and ComplEx have
no relation-on-relation operation that mirrors chaining at all. $\square$
</details>

Every cell of the sheet has a derivation of this size — walk them:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w4-patterns.html >}}

Two consequences worth pulling out of the table. First, the **1-to-N crush** you
watched in Figure 1: any *functional* scorer — one that maps $h$ to a single target
point ($\mathbf{h}+\mathbf{r}$, or $\mathbf{h} \circ \mathbf{r}$) — must place all
of a head's true tails at that one point, so *Tatarstan contains {Kazan, Innopolis}*
forcibly merges the two cities. Similarity scorers (DistMult, ComplEx) can love many
tails at once. Second, a corollary that answers the hero figure:

::: {#cor-transitive .corollary name="Nobody here represents transitivity"}
A transitive relation composes *with itself into itself*: $r \circ r \Rightarrow r$.
TransE then needs $\mathbf{r} + \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}$, i.e. $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}$;
RotatE needs every phase to satisfy $2\theta_i = \theta_i$, i.e. $\theta_i = 0$ — the
identity rotation. Either way the relation degenerates. *located_in* is transitive —
so the hero fact can earn partial credit from geometry, but no exact representation
exists in this family. (Week 5's query embeddings attack multi-hop inference head-on.)
:::

This is the cheat sheet's real lesson: **model selection is pattern audit.** List the
patterns your relations obey — Lab 4 does this for FB15k-237 — and the table picks
your model. No benchmark scores required.

## 5. Training on missing truth

The loss must work under the open-world constraint from §1: positives from
$\mathcal{T}$, negatives manufactured. The classic recipe (TransE) is
<span class="term" data-def="Corruption sampling: manufacture a negative from a positive (h,r,t) by replacing the head or the tail with a random entity — (h′,r,t) or (h,r,t′). The standard source of negatives in KG training, honest under the open-world assumption only because collisions with unstated truths are rare.">**corruption**</span>
plus a margin:

$$
\mathcal{L} = \sum_{(h,r,t) \in \mathcal{T}}
\max\bigl(0,\; \gamma - f(h,r,t) + f(h', r, t')\bigr),
$$

where $(h', r, t')$ corrupts head *or* tail uniformly at random. Read it as a
geometric demand: every true triple must outscore its corruption by at least the
margin $\gamma$, and beyond that the loss stops caring — no wasted gradient on
already-easy comparisons. This is Week 3's SGNS instinct in ranking form.

Uniform corruption has a scale problem: with $10^5$ entities, almost every random
corruption is absurd (*Volga located_in university*), scores terribly already, and
teaches nothing. RotatE's fix — **self-adversarial negative sampling** — reweights
sampled negatives by the *model's own current belief* in them:

$$
p(h'_j, r, t'_j) = \frac{\exp \alpha f(h'_j, r, t'_j)}{\sum_k \exp \alpha f(h'_k, r, t'_k)},
$$

used as weights on the negative terms (temperature $\alpha$; no gradient flows through
the weights). Hard, plausible lies get the gradient; absurdities are ignored. Watch the
budget migrate:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w4-negatives.html >}}

The ⚠ in the widget is the open-world bill arriving: corruption sometimes manufactures
a *true* fact and calls it negative. At toy scale you can see it happen; at $10^5$
entities it is rare per batch but systematic — one reason implementations filter
corruptions against the known triple set, and one reason self-adversarial weighting
must be used with care (it actively *hunts* plausible triples, and the most plausible
"lie" is occasionally the truth).

## 6. Scoring the scorer

Evaluation is ranking, and the protocol has enough teeth to deserve its own worked
example. For each test triple, hide the head (then the tail), score every entity in
the vacancy, sort, find the true entity's rank. Report **MRR** (mean reciprocal rank)
and **Hits@K** (fraction with rank ≤ K). One subtlety separates honest numbers from
nonsense:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w4-eval.html >}}

**Filtered** means: before computing the rank, delete every *other* candidate that
forms a known true triple (train or test). The model ranked Russia above Tatarstan for
*(Volga, flows_through, ?)* — and Russia is *correct*, it just wasn't the held-out
fact. Punishing that is measuring your dataset's redundancy, not your model's error.
Run the protocol yourself, on a model that genuinely never saw the test facts:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w4-rank.html >}}

Two community scandals complete your evaluation education, both in this week's
optional readings. **The dataset scandal:** FB15k, the original benchmark, contained
test triples whose *inverses* sat in the training set — *(a, contains, b)* in train,
*(b, located_in, a)* in test — so a one-line rule "invert and look up" rivaled deep
models. FB15k-237 exists because Toutanova & Chen removed the near-duplicate relations;
it is the benchmark Lab 4 uses, and the reason you should reflexively ask "*could a
lookup solve this test set?*" of any benchmark, in any field. **The tie scandal:**
several published models emitted *identical* scores for thousands of candidates, and
evaluation code that placed the true entity first among ties reported inflated MRR —
models looked strong because of a sorting convention. Random tie-breaking is now the
standard. Neither scandal involved fraud; both involved nobody looking.

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 1 · Reading a KG with closed-world eyes" icon="false"}
"The KG has no *treats* edge between this drug and that disease, so there is no
relationship" — under OWA this inference is void, and in biomedical KGs it is the
*discovery target*. Absence licenses nothing. If your downstream logic needs real
negatives (contraindications, disproven links), they must be curated as explicit
facts, not inferred from silence.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 2 · Raw ranking metrics" icon="false"}
Unfiltered MRR punishes the model for knowing true facts that aren't the held-out one
(the figure's Russia). Always state *filtered*, and always ask which flavor a paper
reports — the gap is large on redundant KGs, and "we beat X" across different
protocols is noise.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 3 · Benchmarks a lookup can solve" icon="false"}
FB15k's inverse-relation leak is one instance of a universal failure: test facts
deterministically recoverable from train by a trivial rule. Before trusting any
completion benchmark — or building your train/test split — audit for inverses,
duplicates under relation renaming, and near-synonymous relations. (This is Week 3's
Pitfall 1 wearing a bow tie: the leak is in the *split*, not the walk.)
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 4 · Trusting scores you didn't tie-break" icon="false"}
If a model scores many candidates identically (saturated activations, quantization,
a bug), rank depends on the sort order — and optimistic tie-handling silently inflates
MRR. Check score-tie rates before celebrating; break ties randomly; be suspicious of
leaderboard jumps unaccompanied by ideas.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 5 · Popularity is not truth" icon="false"}
Entities with many facts get trained more, sit in denser neighborhoods, and outrank
rare entities in *every* slot — your completion model reinvents the popularity
contest (degree bias, third week running). Symptoms: tail-entity queries fail;
Hits@10 looks fine on average and is terrible on rare entities. Report performance
stratified by entity frequency, and remember it when the model "discovers" that a
famous protein is linked to everything.
:::

## In this week's lab

[Lab 4](../labs/lab04.qmd) builds TransE and RotatE from scratch in plain PyTorch
(about a hundred lines each) and trains them on FB15k-237, the honest benchmark: you
implement both scoring functions against hand-checkable asserts (the lecture's toy
numbers), write the corruption sampler and margin loss, run filtered evaluation and
reproduce MRR/Hits@10 on a held-out subsample — and then perform this week's signature
experiment: train both models on a small graph rich in *symmetric* relations, and
watch TransE drive its relation vector toward zero while RotatE parks its phases at
π, exactly as @prp-transe-sym predicts. Theory, caught red-handed.

## Required reading

**1 · Bordes, Usunier, Garcia-Durán, Weston & Yakhnenko — *Translating Embeddings for Modeling Multi-relational Data* (NeurIPS 2013).** [proceedings.neurips.cc](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2013/hash/1cecc7a77928ca8133fa24680a88d2f9-Abstract.html)

::: {.reading-annotation}
TransE — the paper that started modern KG embeddings, and a model of economy: one idea
(relation = translation), one loss (the margin ranking you derived today), five pages.
Focus on §2 — scoring function, corruption, margin loss — and on Table 3, where mean
rank and Hits@10 are defined the way the field still evaluates; note the raw-vs-filtered
distinction being born. Skim the comparisons to the older tensor models (SE, RESCAL) on
a first pass.
:::

**2 · Sun, Deng, Nie & Tang — *RotatE: Knowledge Graph Embedding by Relational Rotation in Complex Space* (ICLR 2019).** [arXiv:1902.10197](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.10197)

::: {.reading-annotation}
The strongest direct descendant. Read §3 and Table 1 slowly — it is today's cheat
sheet in its original habitat, and after this lecture you can verify every cell rather
than believe it. Then study §3.3, self-adversarial negative sampling: a training trick
that matters as much as the model, and Figure 3's learned phase histograms — symmetric
relations really do land on π, which Lab 4 reproduces in miniature. Skim the ablation
tables.
:::

**Also see:** Hamilton, *GRL book*, ch. 4 (knowledge graph embeddings; our notation
follows it) · CS224W, "Knowledge Graph Embeddings".

**Optional:** Yang et al., [DistMult](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6575) (ICLR 2015) —
read §2's unified view of translation vs. bilinear models and meet the symmetry flaw at
the source · Trouillon et al., [ComplEx](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.06357) (ICML 2016)
— §§3–4 for the Hermitian trick; accept the linear algebra, keep the scoring function ·
Toutanova & Chen, [Observed vs. Latent Features](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/W15-4007)
(2015) — the FB15k leak, diagnosed; a few pages, read all of it ·
Sun et al., [A Re-evaluation of KG Completion Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.03903)
(ACL 2020) — the tie-breaking scandal; read for permanent leaderboard suspicion.

## Check your understanding

<details><summary>Q1 · Epistemics — Your team ships a KG-backed compliance tool. A regulator asks: "the graph shows no ownership link between company A and sanctioned entity B — can we clear A?" Answer as this lecture would, and name one engineering change that would let the tool say more.</summary>
No: the KG is open-world — a missing edge means *unrecorded*, not *absent*; clearing A
requires evidence of absence, which silence is not. Engineering change: curate explicit
negative facts for the relations that matter (verified "no-ownership" assertions with
provenance), or report completion-model scores *with* the caveat that they rank
plausibility of the positive, never certify its negation. (Bonus: a calibrated "we
have vetted A's neighborhood to depth k" coverage statement is often what the
regulator actually needs.)
</details>

<details><summary>Q2 · Hand computation — With h = (2, 1), r = (1, 3), t = (1, 2): compute the DistMult score both ways. Then with complex h = 1+i, r = i, t = −1+i: compute the ComplEx score both ways. State what each pair of numbers demonstrates.</summary>
DistMult: $2{\cdot}1{\cdot}1 + 1{\cdot}3{\cdot}2 = 8$; swapped
$1{\cdot}1{\cdot}2 + 2{\cdot}3{\cdot}1 = 8$ — identical, demonstrating
@prp-distmult-sym (forced symmetry). ComplEx: $h r \bar t = (1{+}i)(i)(-1{-}i) = 2$,
so $\operatorname{Re} = +2$; swapped: $(-1{+}i)(i)(1{-}i) = -2$, so
$\operatorname{Re} = -2$ — sign flip, demonstrating the antisymmetric channel opened
by $\operatorname{Im}(r) \neq 0$ (@prp-complex). These are the exact panels of the
scorers figure; the midterm changes the numbers.
</details>

<details><summary>Q3 · Model selection — A family-tree KG has spouse (symmetric), parent_of (antisymmetric, 1-to-N), and grandparent_of (the composition of parent_of with itself). Using only the cheat sheet, pick a model and state what each rejected model gets wrong.</summary>
RotatE: spouse needs symmetry (phases π — TransE out by @prp-transe-sym), parent_of
needs antisymmetry (DistMult out by @prp-distmult-sym), grandparent_of needs
composition ($r_{gp} = r_p \circ r_p$ — ComplEx out, no composition). Caveat worth
stating for full marks: parent_of is 1-to-N, which strains RotatE's functional scorer
(children of one parent get squeezed together) — no model in the family is clean on
this KG, and saying *where* your chosen model will hurt is part of the answer.
</details>

<details><summary>Q4 · Prove it — Show from the definitions: (a) if TransE represents a 1-to-N relation exactly, all N tails coincide; (b) if RotatE represents a transitive relation exactly, the relation is the identity rotation. State what (b) implies about located_in.</summary>
(a) Exactness gives $\mathbf{h} + \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{t}_1$ and
$\mathbf{h} + \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{t}_2$ ⇒ $\mathbf{t}_1 = \mathbf{t}_2$: one landing
point. (b) Transitivity is self-composition into itself, so phases must satisfy
$\theta_i + \theta_i \equiv \theta_i \pmod{2\pi}$ ⇒ $\theta_i \equiv 0$: the identity
(@cor-transitive). Hence located_in — transitive in the world — has no exact RotatE
representation with a non-degenerate relation: geometric KG models *approximate*
transitive closure and provably cannot nail it, which is a standing argument for
Week 5's dedicated multi-hop machinery.
</details>

<details><summary>Q5 · Metrics by hand — A test set has two queries. Query 1: true entity at raw rank 4, with two known-true competitors above it. Query 2: raw rank 1. Compute raw and filtered MRR and Hits@1, and state the general inequality between raw and filtered metrics.</summary>
Query 1 filtered rank: $4 - 2 = 2$. Raw MRR $= \tfrac{1}{2}(\tfrac14 + 1) = 0.625$;
filtered MRR $= \tfrac{1}{2}(\tfrac12 + 1) = 0.75$. Hits@1: raw $= 0.5$, filtered
$= 0.5$ (the filter moved rank 4→2, not to 1). In general filtered ≥ raw for every
query (removing competitors can only improve a rank), so filtered MRR/Hits@K dominate
raw — which is why the two must never be compared across papers.
</details>

<details><summary>Q6 · The leak — Explain the FB15k exploit concretely: what rule solves a leaked test triple, why does an embedding model "learn" it anyway, and how does FB15k-237 close the hole? Connect to Week 3's Pitfall 1.</summary>
If train has $(a, r_1, b)$ and test has $(b, r_2, a)$ with $r_2$ the inverse relation
of $r_1$, the rule "answer with the train partner" is perfect — no learning involved.
An embedding model achieves the same by learning $\mathbf{r}_2 \approx$ the inverse
transform of $\mathbf{r}_1$ (cheap: @prp-rotate's inversion row), so its score
reflects dataset redundancy, not inference. FB15k-237 drops near-inverse/duplicate
relations so no such rule survives. The family resemblance to Week 3: in both cases
test information reaches training through the *data pipeline* (walks across test
edges; inverse triples in train), not through the model — audit the split, not the
architecture.
</details>

<details><summary>Q7 · Self-adversarial — Why does weighting negatives by the model's own scores accelerate training, when the same scores are exactly what training is trying to fix? And name the failure mode the ⚠ candidate in Figure 3 warns about, plus its standard mitigation.</summary>
The margin loss only learns from violated comparisons; uniform corruption mostly draws
absurdities that are already separated, contributing zero gradient. Weighting by
current scores concentrates the batch on the frontier — negatives the *current* model
finds plausible — which is where gradient exists. It is a curriculum generated by the
model itself (and the weights carry no gradient, so it does not chase its own tail).
Failure mode: the most "plausible lie" is sometimes an unstated truth (open world!),
and self-adversarial weighting actively promotes it to chief negative — training then
pushes a true fact down hard. Mitigation: filter candidate corruptions against all
known triples, and keep α moderate so the weighting stays a tilt, not a spotlight.
</details>

## Where this leaves us

Facts became geometry today: relations turned into translations, weightings, and
rotations, and you can now prove — not recall — which regularities each geometry can
hold, train one honestly on positives-plus-silence, and evaluate it without flattering
yourself. You also collected two permanent reflexes: ask what a missing edge means,
and ask whether a lookup could ace the benchmark.

But look at what our best models still cannot do. The hero fact needed *two* hops and
already strained everything (@cor-transitive); a real question — "which drugs target
proteins associated with this disease?" — is a *path with variables in the middle*,
marching through an incomplete graph where every hop might be a missing edge. Chaining
single-hop completions multiplies error; enumerating intermediate candidates explodes.
Next week, queries themselves become geometric objects — boxes that intersect, regions
that contain answers — and the knowledge graph meets the technology that suddenly made
all of this front-page relevant: retrieval for large language models. Bring the
open-world assumption; it is about to become a product requirement.
